speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF DECLARATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to ask all Members of the House of Commons and all Canadians to join with me in celebrating the 40th anniversary of Canadian citizenship.

The Canadian Citizenship Act came into force on January 1, 1947. Before that day we could say we were Canadian citizens, but there was no legal definition of this status. In fact, legally, we were British subjects.

Our concept of citizenship is relatively new and still changing to reflect the realities of this nation. However, I think all Members of this House will agree when I say that three of the fundamental principles of Canadian citizenship are equality, diversity and community. Our Citizenship Act makes equality a basic tenet of the law. It makes no distinction between citizens by birth and citizens by choice, as do many nations. It also treats the citizenship status of women in their own right rather than simply in relation to that of their spouses. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms defines our national commitment to diversity; respect for the heritage and values of the many cultural groups which enrich the Canadian personality. New Canadians are encouraged to retain their heritage when they accept the responsibilities and rights of Canadian citizenship.

Community spirit is that which prompts us to promote the well-being of others and contribute to the growth and expansion of Canada as a whole. Evidence of this can be seen in all regions of the country.
So we do have many reasons to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Canadian citizenship. I urge all Canadians to organize and take part in various activities in their regions. It does not matter much whether it be a festivity, an exhibition or a show, the main thing is to celebrate Canadian citizenship together.

I hope all Members will get involved, work with groups in their ridings and plan and hold celebrations, particularly during Citizenship Week in April and on Canada Day. As parliamentarians we can teach much and we can learn much about what Canadian citizenship is all about. To assist members my department has produced a planning guide to help community groups organize local events. The guide is available from the Department of the Secretary of State or through the 28 citizenship courts across Canada.

The concept of citizenship may be relatively new in Canada, but it has certainly evolved over time. This being an anniversary year, I intend to introduce amendments to make the Citizenship Act even newer.

While most of these amendments will be of a housekeeping nature, I believe a preamble to an amended Act would

January 29, 1987
statements by Ministers
reaffirm the citizenship principles so important to all Canadians. I will be asking Members of this House and groups across Canada to consider what those principles should be since it is very important that Canadians define them themselves.
I hope we will use this 40th anniversary of the Citizenship Act to increase public understanding of, and reaffirm our commitment too, a dynamic multicultural society and a great country.

subsubtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF DECLARATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF DECLARATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to be a Canadian citizen is one of the greatest privileges in this world. I know because I became a Canadian citizen. Millions of people in Canada have done so and there are many who are awaiting to attain that privilege. I am sure as well that there are tens of millions of people in this world who would love to be living in this country and have the privilege and honour of being Canadians.
Citizenship is a relatively new concept in Canada. Canadians have had that special privilege for only 40 years. We should be more concerned about recognizing the importance of being a Canadian citizen. We should celebrate when people have the privilege of becoming a citizen bestowed upon them. We should do more to emphasize its meaning and the responsibilities which it entails, not only for those who become Canadians but for those who are already Canadians.
Other nations understand the privilege and importance of being citizens of their country. The bestowing of an honorary citizenship is the highest honour a nation can give. That is why I enjoyed the privilege of working on a resolution of the House of Commons to bestow an honorary citizenship of Canada upon Raoul Wallenberg for his great achievements on behalf of the human race of saving tens of thousands of lives. The highest recognition that Canada could give was for the House of Commons to pass a resolution supported by all Parties to bestow citizenship upon him. No amount of money and no gift could be as meaningful as the gift of citizenship of Canada. Raoul Wallenberg became the first honorary citizen of Canada.
There are two matters which concern me. The first is that many people who are now elderly came to this country, spent their lives building this nation, and raised their families here. They would like to feel that they belong in this country now. They may not have attained the linguistic requirements which were demanded of them in their earlier years and, therefore, did not become Canadians. They would like to become Canadians in their older years but are hesitant. They feel that there are barriers and requirements which they cannot meet. It would be helpful if the Hon. Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) would reach out to these people to let them know that they need only present themselves and indicate their love for their country and their desire for citizenship. I know that efforts in this regard would be greatly welcomed by the
families of these elderly people who gave of their lives for this country and would now like to have the honour of finally becoming Canadians.
The other matter which concerns me is citizenship court judges. It is sad that we have some negative images of them because of the behaviour of several of these judges. I believe that a great effort should be made to enhance their image, to show the importance of their work, and to accord them the respect that is accorded to other judges. They should be respected so that people can look upon them as friends and people who play their important role in our country. I believe there should be training programs given to new judges to ensure that they conduct themselves in a reputable manner which will give those who are applying for citizenship a good image of our country. We should do everything we can to improve the quality of the service of citizenship judges as well as improving their image in the eyes of those who come before them.
In conclusion, we should think of citizenship in the words of the late President Kennedy of the United States who said those famous words which certainly apply to the people who contemplate their citizenship in Canada. He said: "Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country".

subsubtopic: FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF DECLARATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to be able to join in this brief discussion on the fortieth anniversary of the Canadian Citizenship Act on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic caucus and as spokesperson for multiculturalism in our caucus.
Citizenship represents the personal involvement of members of the Canadian community with the nation. It defines the individual experience of Canadian nationality. The Canadian nation came very slowly to this assertion of its existence as distinct on the face of the globe. It was only in the eightieth year of Canadian Confederation that an Act stated the distinct experience of this nationality. For years preceding, those who had lived in the Dominion of Canada regarded themselves primarily as subjects of the British monarch and members of the Empire, although they did realize that they lived in a distinct country within that Empire that had begun to foster a sense of nationality.
Those who came to Canada from other countries in the years preceding the Citizenship Act of 1947 and were naturalized valued their naturalization papers. However, it was only in that eightieth year that the Canadian Parliament passed an Act which established the reality of Canadian citizenship. It was a citizenship in which all were equal. As the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) has pointed out so well, the act of choosing to come to Canada and becoming a citizen made one as much a member of the family as if one had been fortunate enough to be born into an existing Canadian family and grow up here. There may have been a need for growing in experience, but there was no distinction in law.
January 29, 1987

As the Minister has also pointed out, the experience of women was a primary and individual experience of Canadian citizenship, whatever the status of their spouses might be. Those realities very well anticipated the sensitivity to equality and human rights which Canadians have been fostering in the past few years.
It is in the context of the development of Canadian citizenship that I value the opportunity to participate in citizenship court proceedings in Thunder Bay. As a Member of Parliament I have had the opportunity to attend a number of times. I regard each of these as a very special opportunity. I join in the experience of watching new citizens swear or affirm, according to their own choice, allegiance to the Queen of Canada and to accept the responsibilities and recognize the rights which they now have as new Canadian citizens. When I have the opportunity, as a Member of Parliament, to speak about the rights and opportunities which they now have to partake in Canadian life.
I personally appreciate what Canadian citizenship means.
We have made a commendable advance in Canadian citizenship by expecting all who come to Canada to become citizens in order to vote. The decision to require those who come from the British Isles, the quintessential British subjects, to take out citizenship before they can vote, was the proper decision in an effort to attain full equality.
As we contemplate the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explore the implications of diversity for this country, we appreciate the words of Section 27 which say:
This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
I know that citizenship will be developed and experienced by Canadians in recognition of this diversity. We will cultivate this diversity. We will enrich the cultural life of the country with elements from all over the globe. We will strengthen our national life with these various elements of our heritage and our Canadian citizenship will be enriched in the process.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the Third Report of the Standing

January 29, 1987

Committee on Communications and Culture in the two officials languages.
That report is entitled Federal Museum Policy. The committee request that the Government respond to that report pursuant to S.O. 99(2).
Our report on the federal museum policy stems from the consideration of important matters of Canadian cultural policy undertaken by the committee.

The committee concurs with the recommendation of the National Museums Task Force that new legislation be introduced to establish the four major federal museums as autonomous institutions. The committee feels strongly that the granting programs to non-federal museums should be administered at arm's length, in accordance with the established and well-founded relationship between government and its cultural agencies.
The standing committee also recommends that the administrative costs of the four autonomous federal museums must be kept within the level of financial resources currently allocated to the National Museums of Canada for that purpose.

The federal Government should keep playing a major role in the area of museums, without neglecting to consult the main parties involved. To that end, the Committee recommends that the federal Government develop a new museum policy in consultation with the provinces and the museums community.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank representatives of all parties in this House for their sustained effort in having this unanimous report ready to be presented to the House. I also want to thank all the staff of the Committee for their commitment.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, January 28, 1987, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Benjamin (p. 2756).

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I have I think, three or four minutes left from my speech of yesterday. 1 thought I should return to the House as a matter of courtesy, to make Hon. Members endure another three minutes, and to be available for questioning. Hopefully, there will not be any.
Let me just summarize my objections to this Bill to deregulate transporation. I do not believe Canadians want the Government to control all aspects of their lives. I agree with some Hon. Members of the Government who have said that. However, having said that, I think Canadians need and believe they need strong laws and enforcement to protect their health and safety. This Bill follows blindly the Americans in their deregulation, which has produced some scandals, such as the treatment of older people in nursing homes, in anti-safety measures, anti-health measures and so on, which have come about. If that is what the Government means by "deregulation", I do not believe the people of Canada want it.
Deregulation sounds like a good idea and in some respects it can be. However, with respect to rail or airline safety, I am not so sure it is a good idea. Why should the corporations escape
responsibility to the public and public authorities in these particular areas? If we let the large corporations, the large banks, railway companies and airlines operate without regulations, they will find more and more ways to take advantage of both their employees and the ordinary consumer. Government regulation in Canada has ensured that Canadians are provided with services such as transportation and communication at a fair cost. With this kind of Conservative deregulation, corporations may choose to serve only highly profitable areas and wealthy customers, forgetting about the rest of us.
Let me say that I find this Bill anti-competitive, anti-safety and anti-service. I say it is anti-competitive in that we will have a few companies which will have all of the market, or at least most of it. We already have two airline companies which control 90 per cent of the market now. This Bill does not deal with the problem of the lack of competition.

Second, I find this legislation anti-safety. It is easy to see what can happen when we pick winners and losers, when one airline takes over another that is going under. What we see is the cutting of safety measures. I cited the example of the Arrow Airlines case in Newfoundland where they wanted to cut de-icing procedures to save money. They wanted to overfill the plane, and they did overfill it. There was also a bad record in terms of inspections. That is a good example of what happened with the United States in terms of anti-safety.
I cited articles in my speech yesterday from Time magazine and Business Week with respect to the problems of airline safety in the United States where there are overworked controllers. There were also a number of near misses. There are accidents just waiting to happen.
Finally, I would like to deal with the issue of anti-service. Canadians have had pretty good service and now, for what I think are ideological reasons, to follow blindly the United States to be trendy in this area of deregulation, we will in fact see worse service for Canadians. The Government should remember that Canada is different from the United States. We are not the fifty-first state. We have a history of Crown corporations and a history of laws that protect the safety, service and fairness among companies competing for the business of the ordinary Canadian. Canadians will not stand for a system in which the Government changes its policies to follow blindly the Americans simply to feather the nests of its rich friends in the business community. That is what Canadians believe. That is why we will see some opposition to this Bill.
I want to conclude by saying that I think this is a perfect Bill for a legislative committee to study with hearings across Canada. I heard a motion earlier today about a committee travelling to New York, and other committees looking at different aspects of foreign trade. This Bill deals with something which really affects Canadians in their day-to-day lives. I think the Government should allow a legislative committee to
January 29, 1987

travel across Canada and to hold hearings with respect to this particular Bill. If the Bill is as good as the Government says it is, then there is nothing to fear from ordinary Canadians.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened intently this morning to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). Yesterday I had the opportunity of catching a few of his comments on television, although I was not in the House. I was pleased to hear the Hon. Member say this morning that he thought that deregulation could be a very good thing. That statement gave me heart and encouragement. However, I was disappointed in the bulk of the Hon. Member's remarks this morning.
He talked about this legislation being anti-competitive, antisafety and anti-service. As Hon. Members are well aware, that is certainly not the case. The Bill deals specifically with the question of competition. It does not deal with the question of competition between different modes of transportation, but it deals with trying to promote more competition within each mode. An example of that is with respect to having confidential contracts for rail transportation which will allow for more competition than exists right now. Right now a take-it-or-leave-it situation is being foisted on the public in terms of rail transportation. Once there are confidential contracts and agreements then there will be more competition. I think that is quite clear. I cannot understand why the Hon. Member suggests that this in any way, shape or form is an anticompetitive Bill.
The Hon. Member then went on to say that the Bill is antisafety.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Does the Hon. Member have a question?
Mr. Red way: Yes, I have a question, which I am coming to, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member says the Bill is anti-safety and cites an example with respect to nursing homes. This legislation has nothing to do with regulating or deregulating nursing homes, so there is no question about that issue at all.
It has been indicated that members of the NDP and the Canadian Labour Congress feel that the deregulation policy in transportation may well affect the employment situation in that sector. Will the Hon. Member comment on the fact that between the years 1980 and 1985, when deregulation took place in the United States, employment in the air transportation industry actually increased by some 9 per cent and employment in the trucking industry actually increased by some 22 per cent, even though the United States was experiencing a substantial recession at that time? Does that not undermine the argument that this measure will have a negative effect on employment in the transportation field?

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I draw the Hon. Member's attention to the December 22, 1986 issue of Business Week, in particular to an article entitled, "Is Deregulation Working?
National Transportation Act, 1986
True, Prices Have Fallen but the Top Players May Stifle Competition". Business Week is hardly a socialist magazine. This particular issue talks about the problem with the lack of competition.
I also understand that in the United States there are now fewer air traffic controllers than there used to be, which is one of the problems that country faces. The air traffic controllers are overworked, and some people say underpaid and undertrained. In this respect I draw the Hon. Member's attention to the January 12, 1987 issue of Time in which there is an article on air travel in the United States. The article points out that the number of controllers is down from 16,300 to 14,700 since President Reagan fired striking air traffic controllers. The article points out that only 62 per cent of controllers are qualified at full performance levels versus 80 per cent before the strike. United Airlines Captain Mel Hoagland declares bluntly: "The air-traffic-control system is at the ragged edge of coming unravelled for lack of fully qualified controllers."
We do not want such a system in Canada. We like the Canadian system. We believe in-and do I dare use the word-conserving a good system.
At the beginning of the Hon. Member's comment he said that he was glad to see that I was not against deregulation. I am not against deregulation or privatization per se. I do not want big Government telling Canadians that they have to fill out forms or that it will look after every aspect of their lives. I want ordinary Canadians to have power over their lives. That is what I would like to see. The problem is that we have to be careful in this area.
I tell the Hon. Member that what happens with these types of government Bills is that they shift the power in certain areas in which Canadians want some regulation in safety, health, competition and so on. In those areas Canadians want some regulation. The Hon. Member makes a mistake to follow so quickly the Americans in getting totally rid of regulation. Something which often happens in these cases is that the big guys benefit. They become sort of self-regulated. What they end up doing after some decrease in fares is that they put up the fares because they control the whole market, and they have fewer safety standards.
The Hon. Member should consider the Arrow case. It is a good example of an airline in the United States which, when it was going down, had difficulties in a deregulated environment. It had to cut corners. So they may cut de-icing and save $1,500, take larger loads, or not let their pilots rest. They may cut staff and get more work out of their pilots, or the engineers on a rail train in Alberta. Then accidents happen and people die. Canadians do not want that. That is why they wish to look at this Bill very carefully.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to address the House on Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation. Once enacted this transportation legislation will serve Canadians and the Canadian industry through a new and exciting era in transportation. Canada has reached a critical juncture in its transportation history. We must now position ourselves to optimize our growth and develop potential to respond to a very competive world economy. Canada's existing National Transportation Act is now some 20 years old. It served Canadians well through the years, but the time has come to restructure our legislative framework to respond to the dynamics of the international business world, and recognize the fundamental changes experienced by our own economy.
We have listened to the strong signals for changes to Canada's regulatory regime which emanate from all factors and facets of the transportation community. These signals call for a major restructuring of our transportation legislation; changes which recognize tremendous competition in international trading markets, changes in the regulatory environment in the United States, and new operating and technological developments in Canada. We cannot afford to stand still. Transportation is a fundamental and critical element of Canadian business. Reforms to our legislation are critical in meeting the real challenges faced by Canadian industry and realizing our country's potential. Bill C-18 will provide Canadian industry with this opportunity.
Bill C-18 is best characterized by the two words competition and opportunity. This legislation will promote greater competition in the transportation industry, an initiative which will translate into better prices and services for Canadian travellers and producers. These objectives are of particular significance to western Canada where transportation costs are of vital importance to the survival of resource industries that are competing in a tough international market.
The Canadian economy is continually exposed to greater competitive forces; competition from our traditional trading partners, and ever increasingly from developing nations of the Third World, and those of the East Bloc. Canadian producers are neither sheltered nor shielded from such competition. Daily our industries must compete with producers benefiting from lower production costs, and in some cases cheaper wages and equipment costs. Canadian producers or shippers are keenly aware of the competitive pressures in the market-place and must either respond to them, or withdraw.
In the interests of promoting a responsive, cheaper, and effective transportation service for Canadian travellers and shippers, an increased degree of competition will be introduced into the Canadian transport industry. Bill C-18 does not represent a three-headed monster formulated to scuttle Canada's transportation system. It is a balanced and reasoned approach to the current situation faced by Canada's carriers, and the users of Canada's transportation service.
In June, 1985 the Government released a discussion paper entitled Freedom to Move. This outlined the Government's perspective on the need for change in the legislation governing all modes of transportation. I wish to quote from that paper:
We are a trading nation that must export in order to grow and prosper. It is therefore crucial for our economic well-being that we maintain an efficient, responsive and productive transportation system.
A movement to deregulation has occurred in the United States, Canada's major trading partner. Greatly increased domestic and international competition has become a fact of life for Canadian producers and manufacturers.
On June 26, 1986 the former Minister of Transport, the Hon. Don Mazankowski, introduced two Bills into the House of Commons. Both were designed to introduce greater competition in the transportation industry. I might add that this was the culmination of a great deal of hard work by the former Minister of Transport, and he is to be lauded for this initiative.
This legislative package was aimed at increasing Canada's ability to expand its trade, and thereby increase production and employment. The legislation we are debating today has grown from one of those Bills. It has been refined through the consultative process and revised, where warranted, without sacrificing the principle of increased competition in the transportation industry.
Canada has traditionally been an open economy that is significantly dependent on trade as an engine of growth. In every year from 1980 to 1985 exports ranged around 25 per cent of the Gross National Product. During this period the Gross National Product increased from over $300 billion to over $460 billion, an increase in excess of 50 per cent. In the same period total exports increased from $77 billion to $120 billion, or 55 per cent of the Gross National Product.
While total export growth kept pace with economic growth, the same was not true of exports to particular markets. In current dollar terms, Canadian domestic exports to the United States increased by 92 per cent, but our exports to all other markets combined actually decreased by 7 per cent. We must ask ourselves what happened. The reasons are many. One of the more important factors was the decline in value of the Canadian dollar relative to that of the United States which made us more competitive in the United States' market. Another factor was that the value of the currencies of Canada's competitors declined still further relative to both the United States' dollar and our own.
The Canadian dollar has significantly appreciated relative to other currencies, particularly certain European currencies. For example, our currency appreciated 42 per cent relative to Sweden, 30 per cent relative to Finland, providing those two Scandinavian countries with enormous competitive advantage over Canada, particularly for forest products in European markets. The performance of the Canadian dollar relative to the pound, the franc, and the mark was similar, with the high value of our currency virtually eroding our competitiveness. The recent resurgence of certain European currencies relative
January 29, 1987

to our own is barely sufficient to restore our previous competitive stance.
In short, because of the relative strength of our dollar, Canada faces substantial difficulties in retaining traditional markets, and may experience difficulties in penetrating new markets. It is difficult to remain competitive in world markets when that much ground is lost to competitors on currency exchange alone.
Therefore, Canadian producers must exploit every resource available to them to stay competitive. They must ensure that every aspect to getting goods to market works as efficiently, and I stress, as cost-effectively as possible. This includes the transportation network that links us to those markets.
Clearly we have become far more dependent upon the U.S. market, one of the few major export markets left open to us. In October 1980 the Congress of the United States enacted the Staggers Rail Act of 1980, which radically altered the regulation of railways in that country. That Act encouraged competition between U.S. railroads and stopped the practice of collective pricing by railroads. Confidential contracting for rail services and legalized rebates on published tariffs were introduced and are extensively used. U.S. railroads began to compete vigorously with each other, with trucking, barge and even shipping companies on the basis of price and service. Those able to offer service at the best price prosper at the expense of those who cannot. This has led to a lower level of freight rate.
The Staggers Act had important effects in Canada. First, Canadian railways complained that they were being competitively disadvantaged relative to their U.S. counterparts. Current Canadian legislation did not permit Canadian railways to enter into rebate or confidential contract agreements. Both contracts and rebates were, however, finding their way into Canada via transborder joint through rates with U.S. carriers and U.S. subsidiaries of Canadian carriers. In hearings before the Canadian Transport Commission, Canadian railways claimed to have lost $100 million in revenue due to the competitive disadvantage they suffered visa-vis American railroads.
I believe the railways are pleased with the confidential contract provisions of Bill C-18 as they apply to transboarder rates. They will eliminate this competitive disadvantage relative to U.S. railroads and provide our railways with an opportunity to regain ground lost to U.S. carriers.
Recent developments indicate that Canada's railways are overcoming their reluctance to compete for traffic. Markets virtually controlled by one railway will be exposed to competition. I am confident that our railways will respond to the challenge of competition.
National Transportation Act, 1986
Since Staggers, a number of Canadian shippers have become aware of the opportunity to realize savings in transportation costs using U.S. rail carriers to a greater extent and have devised methods to access them.
Canadian shippers are currently pursuing options to truck products to United States carriers for furtherance by rail to U.S. destinations. We have heard of one shipper who has seriously evaluated the possibility of pipelining his product to a U.S. railroad located just south of the Canada-U.S. border, to be loaded on a U.S. railroad for delivery to U.S. destinations. We must recognize that today, under present transportation legislation, shippers are disregarding traditional transportation solutions and devoting much time and effort to develop innovative and competitive transportation systems to get across the Canada-U.S. border. In many cases these solutions amount to a short hauling of Canadian railways.
Why are shippers resorting to these tactics? We have made some comparisons to help explain this phenomenon. I would be the first to concede that these comparisons are rough. Exact comparisons are most difficult with numbers produced under the auspices of two different Governments for two different countries. However, the indications are most clear that Canadian railway pricing has not remained competitive with that of U.S. counterparts.
In the pre-Staggers period from 1978 to 1980, the annual revenue per tonne for major commodities carried by U.S. and Canadian railways increased at virtually the same annual rates; close to 10 per cent in each case. However, in the postStaggers period from 1980 to 1984, Canadian railway revenue per tonne increased an average of about 7 per cent, whereas in the U.S. railway it increased by only 3.7 per cent, that is, by just over half the average Canadian rate of increase.
For certain commodities the prices paid to move products on Canadian railways have been even higher. Commodities including coal, lumber, wheat, potash, sulphur, wood-pulp, and newsprint experienced an average aggregate revenue per tonne increase in rail rates of over 30 per cent between 1980 and 1984. By comparison, U.S. rail rates increased by just over 15 per cent in the same period.
Since the passage of the U.S. Staggers Rail Act of 1980, United States carriers have had to compete vigorously with each other on the basis of price and service. This has resulted in more competitive freight rates. Many Canadian shippers who must compete in the U.S. market with U.S. producers of the same product are placed at a competitive disadvantage in that market-place because they must pay higher freight rate costs. Clearly, Canadian railways have not operated in a similar business environment as have U.S. railways since 1980. Relatively speaking, this absence of competition has led to significant increases in transportation costs, costs borne by Canadian shippers.
The importance of reducing costs in today's environment is obvious, particularly for those western Canadian resource industries for whom transportation costs represent a large

January 29, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
portion of their delivered price. Lower transportation costs are vital, especially for shippers whose traditional markets have tightened up enormously in the last several years. Lower transportation costs are vital to the western economy.
What are the implications of this? This is perhaps best illustrated by what happened in the transportation of lumber, a subject which is of vital importance to Canada and one which has certainly received its fair share of attention recently.
In 1985 Canada exported nearly $4 billion worth of lumber to the United States, supplying about 33 per cent of the total American market. Close to 50,000 Canadians are employed in the softwood lumber industry in Canada. Lumber traffic is also extremely important for the revenue of both Canadian railways. In 1984 lumber accounted for close to 8 per cent of total railway revenues or more than $410 million. Lumber is second only to coal as the largest single revenue contributor to the Canadian railways. A large portion of this total lumber movement originates in western Canada and is shipped by rail to the sunbelt, north central and northeastern United States. Because of the long distance involved, weights, value of product, et cetera, lumber lends itself well to transportation by rail.
Nonetheless, an analysis of western Canadian lumber shipments to the U.S. over the last five years indicates that there has been a continuing and growing shift from rail to truck, which has been both substantial and dramatic.
Lumber is a rail oriented commodity, especially for the major markets of the United States. However, the railway portion of western Canadian lumber shipments to U.S. markets has declined each year since passage of the Staggers Act. In the same period, the proportion of western Canadian lumber shipments shipped by truck to U.S. markets has increased almost threefold, a rather significant change.
How many millions of dollars of forgone railway revenue does this represent? How many railway jobs has this reluctance or inability to compete cost?
I am not suggesting that healthy intermodal competition between motor vehicles and railways be discouraged. However, I am advised that rail has shown a marked inability to compete in some western transportation markets. What has happened to this traffic? A small portion of this lumber is being trucked to destination, some of it to U.S. ports by container. However, the bulk of the tonnage is not trucked to ultimate destinations. The majority of this traffic is only trucked to, or across the Canada-U.S. border to reload centres for U.S. railroad carriers, for onward movement to U.S. destinations. As we can see, just as water always seeks the lowest levels and finds its own way to get there, traffic managers seek the lowest levels of freight rates and, as I have illustrated, a lot of them also find a way to get there.
Intermodal rail competition for these shippers will only be realized through effective competitive rail access provisions. No effective alternatives to these competitive access provisions
have been found which will provide competitive rail service to these shippers.
These provisions have been greeted with almost universal approval and support of the shipping community.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, the Government maintains that no carrier need necessarily lose long haul movement if that carrier is willing to price competitively. In other words, if a railway is prepared to be competitive, we are convinced that no other railway will be in a better position to meet that rate than the carrier to which the shipper is captive.
Members will undoubtedly have heard that certain measures in Bill C-18 will expose hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian freight traffic to U.S. carriers. The key word here is exposure to loss, not necessarily loss. Loss will only occur if Canadian carriers are non-competitive. Is that not the kind of competition Canadian industries face each and every day?
The benefits of increased competition among U.S. railways have been actively sought by Canadian shippers. For many shippers, lower transportation costs are the key to remaining competitive in world markets. It is now time to bring the benefits of increased competition to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a special interest in this Bill because, when I was Minister of Transport, I began to develop new regulations for the transport industry in Canada. At the time, Mr. Speaker, I had recognized the existence of a serious problem, especially as concerns the lack of flexibility in the rules and regulations. There was no competition to help consumers and producers. I agree with the comments of the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) who said that it is a problem to have the railroads fix set prices for small businesses in Western Canada and other regions.
However, I do have some reservations, Mr. Speaker. I believe that it is important to use caution when making changes in our transport system. At the time, I referred a number of questions to committees of the House of Commons for consideration, including safety, labour management relations, and the role of Crown corporations under deregulation.
Mr. Speaker, after the election in 1984, the Conservative Government dropped all the questions that had been referred. This means that the regions, consumers and producers have not had a chance to examine them and express their views on these very important changes.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill is weak because it ignores the concerns and the views of all Canadians.

There is no question that our transportation system is essential to our health and vitality as a nation. We have always recognized that, with our geography, if we made a mistake in our transportation system we would suffer drastically in our attempts to keep the country together, serve world markets, and develop the dynamism in our economic system that we require. There is no doubt that from time to time major changes have to take place. However, those changes should not be driven by some ideological imperative, but by a clear and careful judgment of what is going to work well.
When I initiated the movement, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said, to change the rules governing airlines, there was incredible opposition from civil servants, the CTC and transportation companies themselves. Everyone said it could not and should not be done. It was a very happy and cosy little club. However, decisions were taking far too long. There was no sensitive response to local conditions. Certainly there was no market-place dynamism which would allow prices to respond to supply and demand.
It is quite true that at that time, in comparison with many other countries, our airline system was in a deep decline. The number of passengers was falling off because we did not have the incentive to broaden the base of people who could afford to fly. The system was catering to the business traveller, Members of Parliament and Senators who do not have to pay for their own tickets because they have expense accounts. For the general public at large air travel was becoming a less attractive
option. That is when we brought in a new airline policy, and I would remind Members of the House that that policy is still in place today. The new Conservative Government has not changed it. Legislation is in front of us now, but changes have not been made to break down the regional divisions and allow airlines a much freer pricing system, or elimination of the conditions of licensing which set rigorous requirements on too many air carriers.
We also initiated discussions with the provinces on changing the rules governing trucking. Consensus was reached on the need for changes in this area at a federal-provincial conference in April, 1984. The legislation before us has an important history, a history with which I associate myself. However, I ask why the progress made up to that point in time was blocked. In effect we were deflected away from something that should have had the basic agreement of all political parties. Instead we had a peculiar partisan move. The Government did not want to be associated with the past initiatives of the Liberal Government so the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) said we were going to do it all over again. However, in doing so, some fundamental mistakes were made. Those mistakes have yet to be corrected. They are not corrected in this Bill or in the policies and programs of the Government and that is why there is such great concern.
The NDP ask why the Liberal Party, which advocated the liberalization of transport in 1984, is critical of this Bill. The reason is that this Bill does not reflect the initiatives, objectives and concerns we raised at that time. Simply because you use the word "deregulation" does not mean that is what it is. I think it is quite correct to say that the Government has adopted, without much thought, the style and methods used in the U.S. It does so in almost everything else, so why not in transportation?
Let me pose a key question. Can you have a fully-deregulated system subject to the discipline of the market-place when you have major Crown corporations still occupying a large part of the market? If you talk to those who have gone through the experience of deregulation their answer is no, of course. If you are going to have a free market you cannot have a government-owned enterprise as a major player in that market. You have to decide what you are going to do with it. If not, you have a hybrid system, one which is highly distorted.
The Government opted for full deregulation but we did not. We carefully used the word "liberalization", a word which is far more compatible to our ears, but it also made more sense because it would allow us to maintain the mixed system we have. This Bill proceeds with a full court press on deregulation. The Government is left with the embarrassing problem of what to do with Air Canada, CNR and VIA Rail. You cannot have a Crown corporation funded by the Government under a deregulated system. No one in the Government has faced that issue. I presume that the previous Minister of Transport was about to face it when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that he could not do anything with it. We all know of the great
January 29, 1987

policy analyses the Prime Minister makes. If he gets through one day without changing his mind it is a small miracle.
The fact is that we now have incredible disharmony that is putting the transportation system out of whack and giving all the wrong signals to the market-place. You cannot say that the private sector is going to make the decisions and still maintain total control over Crown corporations. In addition, the Government has imposed a complete set of restraints upon Crown corporations. Over the past two and a half years the Government has refused to come to grips with the essential financial problems of Air Canada and the CNR. This system has no coherence.
The Government wants to keep Crown corporations but will not give them any money to modernize and respond to the market-place. The private operators do not want the Government to do that anyway because it would be unfair to them. They cannot be subject to the discipline of the market-place where they live and die by supply and demand if one of the big players is government-owned and can always bail itself out by going back to the federal Treasury. We have no formula whatsoever to deal with that fundamental problem.
How can the Government pass a Bill to make the marketplace supreme without coming to grips with what its policy will be in relation to Air Canada and CNR? Will the Government fund them, keep them, partially deprivatize them? What will the Government do? All we get is a great yawning silence from the benches opposite. To proceed with this legislation and the series of principles behind it without coming to grips with that fundamental issue is a recipe for disaster. It will not be a deregulated market-place driven system. It will be hybrid, distorted, and out of whack. We do not know whether the decisions will be made by public sector signals or market signals.
Another fundamental issue which we began to address in 1984 and which has since been wiped off the agenda is that of how to deal with employer-employee relationships. We carefully examined what had happened in other systems under liberalization or deregulation. The crucial issue for many was how to accommodate that change and still maintain effective, proper employer-employee relations. We seem to be adopting the American model of throwing the workers on the scrap heap. That seems to be the system written between the lines in this Bill because nothing else has happened to make any changes.
For example, in 1984 the previous Government was working with various employee groups to make them partners in certain Crown corporations as an incentive. We had started negotiations with several of the major unions and Air Canada. We believed that was one way of solving the serious problem of dislocation. In addition, the problems of harmonizing union rules, seniority, and providing for certain job guarantees must be dealt with. By treating the workers like scrap the Americans created a total lack of morale and disloyalty in the
National Transportation Act, 1986
system. That is why many of those airlines have gone bust. They did not get the productivity, worker involvement, and caring that was required.
In 1984 we gave the simple but important direction that, before proceeding further with any more liberalization or changing of the rules, there must be an agreed upon approach among the unions and employers in transportation with regard to how to deal with worker problems and worker dislocation. Have we heard anything at all from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux)? Has the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) uttered a-

-a word or made the slightest comment on major problems that would have to be considered? None at all.

That is because the Government does not have a policy. It does not know what to do. It has not decided how to come to grips with that fundamental issue.
We have two very major and serious problems which require answers before we can proceed with a fundamental overhaul. The Canadian people, particularly those involved in the transportation industry, are without answers to those questions. It is not as though we in the Opposition have not tried to get answers in committee and other places. However, there has been a stone wall, a refusal to come to grips with those problems.
Do the Conservative Members now in the Chamber have answers to these questions? If so, they should put them forward in the House today. Let us hear what the Conservatives want to do about those two issues. If they do not have answers, they had better not vote for this Bill because that is asking for a pot of trouble. I do not say that for partisan reasons. I say that from experience. I have looked carefully at the issues and, having initiated this in 1984, I can say with some credibility that I knew what to expect.
When the Conservative Government took power and said it was going to continue with this initiative I gave a speech to The Financial Post conference and said, "God bless them, I hope they do well". I was not critical, but said that we should wait and see what they do. We have waited two years and they have not done it right. They have not put it together in the right way.
My colleagues have discussed the Government's policy of ensuring that competition is continued by insisting on fair competition between companies. Instead, we have seen an incredible rash of mergers and acquisitions. How is the Government going to support and stimulate the emergence of commuter and regional airlines to serve small communities?
We shifted allocations in the Department of Transport away from some non-essential expenditure to help smaller private Canadian companies buy new equipment to start up new regional and commuter airlines to serve the Maritimes and the north. One of the first acts of this Government was to wipe out

January 29, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
that support. It did not give those smaller companies an opportunity to get the new equipment they needed to start competing.
That initiative was not a Liberal bogyman. It had worked well in the American system. When larger airlines evacuated a certain market the American Government assisted smaller companies to start up. In the State of Alaska there was an emergence of a number of new regionally based airlines which have been quite successful. The American Government recognized that in order to make that happen there had to be a kick-start, an initial incentive. We had money in our Budget for that. It was not new money. We had reallocated old expenditures. However, the Conservative Government wiped that out.
The Government says that it wants to bring prices down. If that is the case, why has the Government increased user prices for transportation year after year? Why have airport and airline fees gone up? Why have the costs of using ports and dry docks gone up? Why are public charges to the users of the transportation system being increased when the Government says it wants the private sector to bring prices down. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-18, recognizing that it is a Bill designed to bring the Canadian transportation industry and Canadian business and commerce into a more competitive mode of operation. I would like to direct the attention of the House to a particular aspect of Bill C-18, the tough watchdog of safety and public interest, the new national transportation agency which is established under the provisions of Part 1 of the Bill. I trust Hon. Members opposite have addressed themselves to Part 1 of the Bill and that particular agency.
As Hon. Members know, this new agency will replace the Canadian Transport Commission, so that it does become a

January 29, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
replacement agency, yes, but it will operate in a far different way. It will not be a regulatory body in the sense that the old one was. It will, however, be a transportation ombudsman, a mediator and, as I said before, a public watchdog. Its powers allow it to monitor compliance and establish new regulations if the public interest is jeopardized by unsafe practices or a lack of competition. It will have the ability to make inquiries into complaints, establish competitive line rates, grant entry into markets and provide mediation services to help resolve shipper-carrier disputes.
The over-all intent of Bill C-18 is to reduce the regulatory burden on industry and at the same time deal more quickly and effectively with real problems as they emerge. The new agency is uniquely designed to do that. First, the agency has a wider range of options to deal with complaints and disputes between the various modes of transport. Indeed, the main responsibility of the new agency will be to administer a family of dispute resolving mechanisms contained within the bill itself. These include mediation services, a final offer arbitration service, a simplified procedure for investigating complaints from aggrieved parties. All of these provisions are new. They are all designed to assist industry to operate in an environment which is freer of Government regulation and intervention.
Let us look at disputes between a shipper and a carrier for a moment. The new agency, at the request of both parties, will call in a mediator. If the mediator is unsuccesssful in resolving the dispute, and if the shipper requests it, an arbitrator may be appointed. The arbitrator will then choose between the final offers. We used to do that in the practice of law between disputing parties. We would make our best offer and then let the chips fall where they may. The arbitrator makes his decision and, according to the Bill, that decision must remain in effect for a period up to a year. That is enough to prompt each party to make its best offer and enough to encourage shippers and carriers alike to settle their disputes between themselves and without recourse to the agency. However, the agency is there to do it for them.
The same applies to cargo rates and fares. Under the new rules, carriers will be permitted to establish fares and rates without regulatory approval. However, the provision is there for complaints in case of abuse. Increases in regular passenger fares on monopoly routes can be appealed to the National Transportation Agency. If it is determined that the rates are unfair, are being abused or that the increase is unreasonable, the agency can disallow the new fare and order a reduction, with refunds where practical.
The national transportation agency will be smaller and more streamlined than the old Transport Commission. It will have to adhere to time limits when dealing with complaints and applications for new services. The old Board was never constrained in such a manner and as a result those disputes would drag on and on, which was a disservice, not only to the parties to a complaint but to the users as well.
The size of the agency, along with the time limit, will make it far more responsive to the needs of shippers, users, the industry and the public than was the former Canadian Transport Commission. Further, the new agency is given functions and powers specifically tailored to the Government's new policies and approach.
The agency will be bound by policy directions which may be issued by the Governor in Council. Some Hon. Members opposite may say this is political manipulation. I want to point out that, with the provisions in this Act, nothing could be further from the truth. Any policy direction issued to the new agency must first be presented to both Houses of Parliament. Further, as in the normal course of business in the House, a policy direction might be referred to a committee for detailed consideration. What more could one ask than that?
In addition, under the Bill, no policy direction can have any bearing on any specific case before the agency at the time. Government will not be able to intervene in any case being considered by the agency. The legislation is phrased to prevent this type of interference or intervention. It is a protection from the type of allegation that might be made by Members opposite.
Too often there is a type of regulatory capture between a government body and the industry it regulates. The new agency will be structured on a multimodal basis to prevent that. We are talking about deregulation of all modes of transportation just to prevent that type of occurrence. Agency members will deal with the transportation network as a whole rather than the railway component, the airline component or even a marine component. These are separate entities in themselves. This structure is inherently more fair, as well as being more flexible than that found in most government agencies.
Before closing I would like to make the point that while the Canadian Transport Commission itself will be terminated, the Government intends to draw upon the expertise as presently contained within that body in the staffing of the new agency. This intention was clearly stated in the Freedom to Move document, and I can assure Hon. Members that it remains the policy of the Government. While the headquarters of the agency will be in Ottawa, it may also have regional offices across the country to give closer contact with the users and providers of transportation services.
Bill C-18 is an important part of the Government's over-all program to spur economic renewal and create jobs by removing regulatory obstacles. It is a vehicle whereby the transportation sector can renew and strengthen itself. The new agency will play an important role in this effort. With its new responsibilities and structure, with the time-limit on decisions and with a greater responsiveness to government policy the agency will be well designed to foster the development of a first-rate transportation system throughout our land.
January 29, 1987

subtopic: RETENTION OF ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON BY FRANCE
RETENTION OF ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON BY FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 19th century colonialism appears to be alive and well in North America. India has eliminated Portuguese possession of Goa; Hong Kong and Macao will shortly revert to China; and even tiny Iceland has resolutely and successfully defended its exclusive fishing zones against once mighty Great Britain, but France is allowed to maintain its colony of St. Pierre and Miquelon in the midst of Canada.
Surely this is an anachronism in the third quarter of the 20th century. Worst of all, on the basis of this historic relic, France claims the right to catch tens of thousands of tonnes of Canadian fish. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) should start immediately, and as forcefully as possible, to pursue the termination of French colonialism within Canada's domain.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a question of privilege on a decision made at this morning's meeting of the legislative committee dealing with Bill C-22. At one of the first meetings of that committee, a motion was made by a government Member that a quorum of the committee authorized to conduct the work of the committee should consist of four Members. I moved an amendment, which was accepted, voted on and approved, that among the four Members who would constitute a quorum at least one should be a Member of the Opposition. The two members of the Opposition serving on that committee are the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) and myself.
The committee at a later date accepted a motion that the committee should meet five times a week and that at each meeting the committee should hear three delegations, each delegation to have 45 minutes and not more. The Member from East Richmond and I argued that this was too restrictive, but that motion carried.
This morning the committee met to hear two delegations, first, the delegation representing the Multiple Sclerosis Organization of Ottawa. That Organization had its 45 minutes. Then came the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. After about 40 minutes, the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond left. I stayed and when I thought 45 minutes had elapsed, I left. Certainly at the least 43 minutes had gone by.
Just let me go back a step, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday the committee discussed future witnesses. The Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond proposed that we invite Congressman Waxman who heads up a committee looking into this question in the U.S. House of Representatives and I suggested that we invite a representative of the American Association of Retired Persons. I suggested, and it was agreed, that we find out whether either of these individuals could come and whether we would have to pay their expenses. If we did, then we could discuss whether the committee had the funds. That was the way it was left.
As I said, the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond left the committee. Then after I left, believing the time had gone by for the delegation, the committee adopted, without the presence of either member of the Opposition, a motion that no invitation be extended to any possible delegation from the United States. I think moving and passing that motion when

Mr. Speaker, I want to make some very brief comments about this matter. I hope you will take note of the fact that almost every week there is a point of order or question of privilege raised in this House about what some members think are incidents of unfairness in standing and legislative committees. I invite you, Sir, to determine whether or not the time has come for you to use the broad residual authority, which I submit you have, to ensure that committees operate as fairly as the House of Commons itself with regard to members who are in opposition to the Government, as well as members who support it.
With regard to this particular incident, I believe that the normal practice for making decisions with regard to hearing witnesses would be for the matter to be first considered by the steering committee, on which there are representatives of the opposition Parties, and then considered by the full committee with full opportunity for opposition Members to be present, take part in debate on the motion, and vote on it.
Parliament is a court. It is called the High Court of Parliament. There is a basic principle in the British and Canadian judicial systems. That principle is audi alteram partem, hear the other side. With all due respect to the Government majority on the committee which proposed and voted on that motion in the absence of opposition Members, they did not follow that basic principle.
I respectfully submit that this is a very serious matter and it is not being raised for the first time. There is a pattern developing which, if allowed to continue and solidify, will destroy all claims of value in the changes in the rules with respect to the role of members on all sides of this House in the committee system and in the operation of the House of Commons.
In conclusion, at the very least, at the next meeting of the committee it should agree to revoke this motion and refer the matter to the steering committee for a full and fair consideration such as we are accustomed to in the House of Commons and its committees. If this does not happen, I am sure this matter will reappear before you so that we can again invite you to use that residual authority, perhaps a moral authority, which is very much in existence, to ensure that the House of Commons and its committees operate fairly in the interest of all its members, not only those who for the time being are in support of the Government.
